Power & utilities · Rwanda

Structures and vegetation inside power-line rights of way in Rwanda

A dated register of the structures, fresh excavations and tall vegetation inside the rights of way of your transmission and distribution lines, each measured to the centreline against the widths in RURA’s guidelines or in your easement file. For existing lines, new routes and the records a resettlement action plan needs. Satellite first, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Send us your line route See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

A right of way fixed on paper, and land that keeps changing

“There are houses within 6 m of the line we are rebuilding.”

An environmental and social impact assessment REG published for a distribution project in 2024 records the practice: clearance “on 12 meters large (6 m each side from the center line)”, and “a residential house found within the 6 m will be relocated and fair compensation will be done”, with “maximum efforts” in re-route design to avoid houses under the right of way. Those efforts start from knowing where the houses are.

“The easement was agreed years ago.”

RURA’s guidelines require easements to be registered under the land-registration law. They allow gardens, pastures and fences in the right of way with the licensee’s consent. They forbid building or cultivating there without it, and any drilling, mining or excavating in it. A dated record shows what stands there now, next to what was agreed.

“The valuation starts when the decision is published.”

Under the Expropriation Law, long-term activities started on the land after the expropriation decision is published “shall not be compensable” (Law n° 32/2015, art. 17). A record of what stood where, and on which date, matters to everyone at the valuation.

“Our lenders want a cut-off record.”

A 2026 resettlement action plan published by REG for a substation observes that “The Rwanda national law is silent on cut-off date”, and adopts the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standard 5. Lender-financed lines need that date, and what stood in the footprint on it.

Who this is for

  • Network planners and line developers
  • Right-of-way and land officers
  • Resettlement and RAP teams
  • ESIA consultants
  • EPC contractors
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers
  • Distribution roll-out programme teams
  • GIS teams

The rule

The right of way is already defined

A summary of the public rules, last reviewed 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Chapter IX of Law n° 21/2011 governing electricity, unchanged by the 2018 amendment, says: “The right of way is necessary to the operators in production, transmission, distribution and supply of electricity. It shall be exercised in accordance with the standards set by the regulatory agency. Expropriation shall be conducted in accordance with the Law governing expropriation for public interest” (art. 48). Complaints about interference with property, including the right of way, go to the regulator and, if needed, the courts (art. 49).

The standards are RURA’s Guidelines N°01/GL/EL-EWS/RURA/2015 on Right-of-Way for Power Lines, adopted on 30 November 2015: “a safety corridor to allow the Licensee to keep the power lines clear of tall trees, building and other structures that could interfere with line operation”. Distribution lines are those up to 30 kV, transmission lines 110 kV and above. Schedule I sets the minimum widths:

Voltage Right of way Each side
0.4 kV 3 m 1.5 m
15–30 kV 12 m 6 m
110 kV 25 m 12.5 m
220 kV 30 m 15 m
400 kV 50 m 25 m

The widths are minimums. The actual width depends on topography, structure type and span, existing lines “may differ”, and where a line runs beside a road or railway “a lesser width may be required” (II.2). A right of way is acquired by an easement negotiated with the owner, by purchase or by expropriation, and “All easement rights shall be registered in accordance the Law in force governing land registration” (III.1–III.3).

What the guidelines forbid (IV.4)

  • Any building, structure, cultivation, farming or other activity in the right of way “prior to the consent of the Licensee”
  • Drilling, mining or excavating in the right of way
  • Fire “within Sixty (60) meters of the transmission line Right-of-Way”
  • “any form of blasting within hundred (100) meters of any power line”
  • Permanent buildings, pools, septic tanks, dumps, wells, fuel storage and other non-compatible uses

What they allow with consent (IV.5)

Yards, gardens, pastures, farming, roads, fences and similar uses with the licensee’s prior written consent, and small, movable, non-habitable temporary structures with approval. Schedule II adds clearances from petrol tanks and vents (15 m, or 20 m at 400 kV) and from liquid-gas tanks (3 m to 25 m, by tank size and voltage).

That is why we measure each structure against the width for your voltage, or the easement widths in your file, and leave the judgement of what is authorised to you.

Existing lines

A baseline by band and by segment, then what changed

We buffer the line route you supply in its UTM zone at the half-widths for its voltage and list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the centreline, its band, its chainage and its coordinates. For a mixed network that means 6 m, 12.5 m, 15 m and 25 m, with wider context bands, such as 60 m and 100 m, if you want them. Each 500 m stretch is rated for encroachment density, high, medium or low, by a count rule, so your officers know which stretches to visit first. It is not a safety rating.

After the baseline, the line is re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures between dated surveys are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and a notice after each survey says what changed and where. Fresh digging, spoil heaps, new tracks and cleared ground near the line are flagged the same way, so field teams know where to check; they do not replace patrols.

What you receive

  • A register: ID, distance to the centreline, band, chainage and coordinates
  • A density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • The imagery source and date for every feature
  • New and removed structures between surveys
  • Fresh excavation, tracks and cleared ground, flagged for checking
  • A PDF report in English, with GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers that load into your GIS

New lines

Compare routes by the structures they would cross

REG’s transmission development plan (June 2023) records about 1,156 km of high-voltage lines, describes a national grid that is “isolated from the transmission networks of the neighbouring countries or interconnected with a weak link”, and lists new 110 kV and 220 kV lines, planned and funded, for a plan it says is “reviewed every 6 months”. Distribution grows through World Bank-financed access programmes. High- and medium-voltage lines are on the list of projects that need an environmental impact assessment (Ministerial Order of 2018, Annex I).

For each alignment option we count the structures within the 12.5 m and 15 m half-widths of a 110 kV or 220 kV line, and in wider bands if you want them, and screen slope, drainage crossings and flood exposure. Once the route is fixed, a dated register supports the ESIA baseline and the resettlement records.

What a route comparison is

An input to route selection: structures per option and per band, from dated imagery, with the source named. It is not a full alternatives assessment, and it does not promise that a route avoids resettlement.

Route and site selection

Before valuation and RAPs

What stood on each segment, and when

Electric lines are activities of public interest under Law n° 32/2015 on expropriation (art. 5), and the Electricity Law sends expropriation for a right of way to that law (expropriation pour cause d’utilité publique; Kinyarwanda kwimura abantu kubera inyungu rusange). The Expropriation Law’s timeline is short and date-driven:

  • the decision is announced on radio and in a newspaper, and the list of right holders is posted at the City of Kigali, District, Sector and Cell offices (art. 16);
  • after publication, “the land owner shall not develop any other long-term activities on the land. Otherwise, such activities shall not be compensable” (art. 17), a long-term activity being one “likely to remain there for more than one hundred and twenty (120) days” (art. 2);
  • no compensation for activities developed on land where they were prohibited after the relevant laws were enacted (art. 26);
  • valuation within 30 days, extendable by up to 15 days (art. 29), and payment within 120 days of the day the compensation is approved by the District or City of Kigali Council or the relevant Ministry, or the expropriation becomes void unless agreed (art. 36).

A dated inventory of what stood on each segment, and when, supports the record your RAP team needs, and supports cut-off-date records under the World Bank’s ESS5 and IFC Performance Standard 5. Fair compensation (indishyi ikwiye) itself is set by valuation on the ground.

What the record is, and isn’t

  • A dated list of structures in the footprint, with imagery, coordinates and IDs
  • New structures after the date, flagged and confirmed by a reviewer
  • It supports the census and asset inventory; it does not replace them
  • It never establishes ownership, use or value

Vegetation

Tall vegetation and cleared ground in the corridor

The licensee’s duty

The licensee maintains the right of way in the wire and border zones, removes dangerous vegetation, also outside the right of way, sets pruning cycles and notifies the landowner before pruning or clearing (IV.6). The 2024 ESIA quoted above clears only trees and crops that can grow to more than 3 m in its 12 m right of way.

Where tall vegetation stands

Mapped from drone elevation models where flown, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, and from open canopy-height data for wider context. The open data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture. It is not a measured clearance to conductors.

Cleared and regrown ground

Where vegetation in the corridor has been cleared or has grown back between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data. It shows larger patches of change, not single trees, and cloud can delay results.

Vegetation, land cover and fire, in detail

Drones along a line

High-tension lines are restricted sites for drones

Flying a drone at “high tension cables and communication masts” is an offence under art. 100 of Law n° 20/2018 unless it follows the conditions of the restriction or RCAA has given permission, and RCAA’s advisory circular lists power plants among the strategic installations. Every drone survey of a line, substation or power plant therefore needs an RCAA permission that names the line or site, on top of the registration, pilot licence and activity permit Part 27 requires and, where RCAA asks for one, an operator certificate. Over inhabited plots, flights also need the consent of occupiers or owners, or an authority-level consent.

That is why a survey starts from satellite. Where a stretch needs more detail, drone surveys are subject to the RCAA approvals, security reviews and consents each job requires.

Drone law in Rwanda

The Part 27 approvals, restricted sites, BVLOS area approvals and an 11-point checklist for clients, as of 27 September 2026.

How it works

From line route to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the line route, the voltage, pole or tower positions if you have them, any easement widths and what the register is for: maintenance, a new route, an ESIA baseline or a RAP. We agree the bands, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures are mapped along the whole line from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold.

  3. Check up close

    Reviewers mark structures by hand where villages are dense or tree cover is mixed. Drone detail, where needed, is subject to the approvals each flight requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result; each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name.

More on how it works, the methodology, imagery and data sources and power and utilities across our countries.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cleared ground, fresh excavations and tracks visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the centreline, at the Schedule I or easement widths
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated, credited records that support your right-of-way, ESIA and resettlement work

What we don’t do

  • Measure conductor clearances or inspect poles, towers and hardware
  • Detect theft or vandalism, or identify who did anything
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised, or replace a land surveyor
  • Offer field or drone work within 10 km of the DRC border

Frequently asked questions

Which right-of-way widths do you measure?

By default, the minimum widths in Schedule I of RURA’s guidelines, with the line centred, so the half-widths are 6 m for 15–30 kV, 12.5 m for 110 kV, 15 m for 220 kV and 25 m for 400 kV. The guidelines also say existing lines “may differ” and that a lesser width may apply where a line runs beside a road or railway, so send the easement widths in your file where they differ. We can add wider context bands, such as 60 m and 100 m, and report up to six widths in one survey.

Why do you say “right of way” and not “servitude”?

Because in Rwandan land law a servitude is something else. The 2022 Ministerial Order determining types of servitude deals with pathways to a parcel, a well, a river or a lake, between 1 m and 1.5 m wide. For power lines, the Electricity Law and RURA’s guidelines use “right of way” (French droit de passage; Kinyarwanda uburenganzira bwo kubona inzira), secured by an easement, a purchase or expropriation.

Can you tell us which structures are unauthorised?

No. The guidelines say the right of way “shall generally be clear of unauthorized structures”, and they allow some uses, such as gardens, pastures, fences and small movable structures, with the licensee’s prior written consent. Whether a structure has that consent, or predates the line, is for the licensee and the authorities to decide. We show you, with dates, what is there.

Can you measure clearance to conductors?

No. We show where structures and tall vegetation stand in the right of way and how far each is from the centreline. Tall vegetation comes from drone elevation models, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, or open canopy-height data for wider context. None of that is a measured clearance to a conductor, which stays with your line engineers.

Do you detect cable theft or tower vandalism?

No. Satellites and drones see land change, not theft or vandalism. We flag fresh excavation, spoil and works visible at the surface near the line between surveys, so your teams know where to check.

Is the register a cadastral survey?

No. Rwanda’s land register records each parcel’s Unique Parcel Identifier (UPI), location, surface area and cadastral plan extract. Our registers are monitoring and planning records built from imagery, not cadastral surveys; they show your land team and surveyors where to look.

Our line runs close to the DRC border. Can you still help?

We do not offer field or drone work within 10 km of the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in line with current government travel advice. A route that enters that band is scoped without field or drone work on the stretches inside it, and the proposal says so.

Send us your line route

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, with pole or tower positions if you have them, the voltage, the Districts it crosses and any easement widths that differ from Schedule I. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
